title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot NL→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (preregistration rX4f7-1). Using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3, edge vs core breakdown) was not executed by the archived analysis executor; the reported primary inferential results are pooled across the full corpus (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/results.json in the archived artifacts). Representative validator traces and provider audit logs show repair was invoked only three times. Under these controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; we document analytic deviation (use of exact McNemar for paired binary outcomes) and provide archive pointers to permit reproducible follow‑up.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are proposed increasingly to translate operator intent in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and systems work argue that reliability and operational safety emerge from the full orchestration stack—model, verifier, provenance, and sandboxed execution—not from an LLM alone [http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12708/229494, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13389]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidates, an automated verifier enforces syntactic and semantic constraints, and an automated repair step iterates until constraints are satisfied. Despite conceptual consensus, there is little publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence that measures whether verifier assistance produces a reproducible improvement on an operational, rollback‑aware binary success metric relative to a one‑shot pipeline.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench (study_id = rX4f7-1): a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study that compares (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline that reuses the same shared initial candidate per pair to isolate the verifier/repair effect. The preregistered confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Key contributions are: (1) a preregistered experimental design and archived execution artifacts (rX4f7-1); (2) a confirmatory paired analysis on 1,199 complete pairs using the requested model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; and (3) transparent reporting of counts, bootstrap CI, and an analytic deviation (use of an exact McNemar test appropriate for paired binary outcomes). We explicitly note that the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3) was not executed by the archived analysis executor; the primary results reported below are pooled across both simulated topology clusters (edge and core).
sections.related_work:
System and survey literature frames LLMs as components inside AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly emphasizes that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution) rather than of an LLM alone [http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12708/229494, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13389]. Several recent works instantiate generate–validate‑repair patterns for NL→formal translations or topology compilation, demonstrating that automated verifiers can detect syntactic and some semantic errors and drive repairs in constrained settings [https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09369, https://doi.org/10.3390/app16010085]. Other efforts propose “LLM firewalls” and provenance linkers that attempt to detect prompt injection and provenance loss; these works motivate provenance‑rich, audit‑ready benchmarks [https://doi.org/10.3390/info17030297, https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6947162].

Prior demonstrations often evaluate on constructed or limited corpora under domain‑specific validators; reported performance gains therefore depend strongly on task selection and verifier strictness. NetOpsTraceBench implements a preregistered, paired design and archives deterministic task generation, validator traces, and emulator execution to make the dependence of measured gains on corpus and verifier observable and reproducible.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study was preregistered as rX4f7-1 and the preregistration manifest (SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) froze hypotheses, inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Confirmatory hypothesis H1 expected a positive paired advantage for the guarded pipeline; H3 specified a per‑topology confirmatory breakdown (edge vs core).

Task corpus and topology clusters: The benchmark scope defined 1,200 distinct operator‑intent tasks split conceptually into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (generator_version=5.0) with frozen per‑task seeds. Each task payload included initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit required_sequence arrays, workflow_policies, and a declared difficulty label. Tasks carry deterministic provenance tags (synthetic/consented) that feed the contamination checks.

Paired pipeline design and shared_initial_candidate rationale: To isolate the incremental value of verifier/repair from generation variability, the preregistered design used shared_initial_candidate semantics: baseline and guarded episodes for the same task reuse the same first LLM candidate. This paired, shared‑candidate design reduces variance attributable to generation stochasticity and ensures discordant pairs reflect verifier/repair differences rather than differing initial proposals. The shared_initial_candidate choice and its seeds are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*shared-initial.txt) so follow‑up studies can compare independent‑generation designs.

Implementation details: Adapter orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Model calls requested the model gpt-5-mini via provider recorded as openai_responses; execution/model_configuration.json (archived) records requested_model=gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens=1500, maximum_attempts_per_call=1. Per preregistration initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; repair is conditional on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rejecting the initial candidate. The validator performs canonical parsing, enforces workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), emits validation_before/validation_after diagnostics, and sets validation_after.valid. The preregistered binary episode success requires (1) validator acceptance, (2) emulator availability within tolerance, and (3) no automatic rollback during execution.

Contamination, exclusions, and analysis plan: Conservative contamination detection (token/subsequence threshold T_contam = 0.85; optional embedding cosine = 0.92) and deterministic exclusion rules were enforced as preregistered. The primary analysis used complete_pair_primary (exclude flagged pairs); a sensitivity analysis treating excluded pairs as failures was preregistered. The archived confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test for paired binary outcomes and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples; these analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Important preregistered vs archived-analysis note (required revision response): The preregistration included H3 as a confirmatory topology‑cluster breakdown. The archived analysis artifacts produced by the analysis executor contain only the pooled confirmatory analysis across the entire corpus; H3 (per‑cluster confirmatory tests) was not executed by the archived analysis executor and therefore is not reported as a confirmatory result. The archive files documenting the pooled analysis include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, and execution/execution_manifest.json. Researchers who wish to run per‑cluster breakdowns can reproduce them from the archived per‑task manifests (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and the raw episode artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json) under the same frozen seeds and analysis code.
sections.results:
Execution and counts: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199). Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 (completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1) and stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3 (execution/execution_manifest.json; deterministic_reconciliation.json is archived). The small repair count indicates that most shared initial candidates were accepted by the deterministic validator.

Primary paired outcomes (pooled): The 2×2 paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196 (both succeeded), n10 = 3 (guarded only), n01 = 0 (baseline only), n00 = 0 (both failed). Baseline_success_count = 1,196 (baseline_success_rate = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149) and guarded_success_count = 1,199 (guarded_success_rate = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0). Observed paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 (archived in analysis/results.json). The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) is [0.0000, 0.0058381985] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg archived).

Missingness and exclusions: analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 1,199, failed_baseline_episodes = 1, failed_guarded_episodes = 1, both_missing_pairs = 1. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (no pairs flagged by contamination rules). All per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) include normalized_response, validator_trace.validation_after, and score_reason_code recorded for reproducibility.

Repair invocation diagnostics and difficulty labels: The archived task manifests contain declared difficulty labels ("medium", "hard", "very_hard") per task. Representative scoring artifacts (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000002-*.json, task-000003-*.json) show that even tasks labeled "hard" frequently produced initial candidates accepted by deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator_trace fields (observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count) and repair_applied flags are archived for every episode. The repair stage was invoked exactly three times (execution/provider_calls and provider audit), matching the repair count in deterministic_reconciliation.json.

Topology‑cluster (H3) archival status: To be explicit, the preregistered H3 per‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (edge vs core) was not executed by the archived analysis executor; only pooled confirmatory results are present in the archived artifacts. The per‑task manifests and per‑episode scoring artifacts necessary to compute per‑cluster contingency tables are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/scoring/*.json), enabling reproducible post‑hoc per‑cluster analyses but not altering the confirmatory conclusions presented here.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The pooled exact McNemar test (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.25; the paired bootstrap CI includes zero. Two facts explain why the study did not detect a statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline: (1) baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈0.9975), leaving very little absolute headroom; and (2) the task generator plus validator configuration produced many initial candidates that satisfied deterministic intent constraints, so repair was rarely exercised (repair = 3). The preregistered power calculation targeted an MDE = 0.05 under assumed baseline ≈0.70; the observed near‑ceiling baseline reduces power to detect the observed ≈0.0025 absolute gain.

Operational implications and design lessons: Under task sets where initial generations already meet deterministic verifier rules, verifier‑assisted pipelines will be infrequently exercised and measured binary gains will be small. This outcome does not disconfirm the conceptual value of verifiers; rather, it highlights that empirical measurement of verifier benefit depends critically on corpus difficulty, adversariality, and verifier strictness. The shared_initial_candidate paired design reduced generation variance and isolates verifier/repair effects; follow‑ups can vary generation semantics (independent initial draws) and increase adversarial difficulty to enlarge discordant‑pair incidence.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is strong due to frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, and automated exclusion rules. Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) captures operational correctness in production settings. External validity is limited: only the requested model family (gpt-5-mini) was exercised, tasks are synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic, and Mininet‑style emulation may not capture vendor‑specific or routing‑convergence phenomena. Different validator strictness or task adversariality could materially change repair invocation and measured gains.

Reproducibility and follow‑up: All seeds, task-generator code, validator rules, raw model outputs, provider traces, scoring artifacts, and analysis code are archived. Key archived artifacts for the pooled confirmatory result are analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and execution/execution_manifest.json. Per‑task manifests (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) permit reproducible per‑cluster breakdowns or sensitivity runs that vary verifier strictness or corpus adversariality.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench preregistered and executed a paired, emulator‑grounded comparison of one‑shot vs verifier‑assisted NL→config pipelines (study rX4f7-1). In the archived pooled analysis on 1,199 complete pairs using the requested model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, baseline success was 1,196/1,199 and guarded success was 1,199/1,199; the paired difference = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap CI includes zero) and exact McNemar p = 0.25. The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed by the archived analysis executor; per‑cluster confirmatory tests therefore are not reported as confirmatory here, but the archived per‑task artifacts permit reproducible per‑cluster analyses. The dominant empirical lesson is that measured verifier value depends on corpus difficulty and verifier settings: when initial candidates satisfy deterministic checks for well‑specified synthetic tasks, automated repair is rarely invoked and absolute gains on a binary success metric will be small. We release full artifacts and analysis code to enable reproducible sensitivity studies that vary corpus adversariality, verifier strictness, and generation semantics to determine conditions under which verifier scaffolding yields operationally meaningful improvements.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
